title: The Case Against El-Sayed Doomerism - The Bulwark
content: The Associated Press this morning called the Michigan Senate Democratic primary: Abdul El-Sayed won a much closer than expected victory over Haley Stevens. Let’s get under the hood on the numbers to understand if Democrats are taking a big risk on the youngblood. Start with this: El-Sayed should beat Mike Rogers, the former longtime congressman who is the Republican nominee, because Michigan is a fairly Democratic state. The current governor of Michigan is a Democrat and Democrats have held the governorship for 16 of the last 24 years.1 Since 1979, Democrats have held both of Michigan’s Senate seats for the entire period, with the exception of a single Senate term when Spencer Abraham was elected in the 1994 Republican wave. Here are the ten Senate elections since Abraham broke the streak: You can see a clear pattern of Republicans gaining ground since 2014—but Democrats have still performed well. They’ve won open seats; they’ve won in midterm elections when Republicans are surging nationally. They’ve won in presidential years when Republicans captured the White House. They’ve even won an open seat while Trump was carrying the state at the presidential level. What this tells us is that Michigan is a Democratic state. With an open seat, in a good environment for Democrats, without Trump at the top of the ticket, any replacement-level D should win this Senate seat.2 Translation: El-Sayed would have to be worse than a generic Democrat—by at least 1.5 points—in order to lose. He’s an excellent speaker and a real political talent. He ran an insurgent campaign, going from near the rear of the pack to the front. He beat the entire state Democratic establishment that came out to oppose him. That’s a lot of positives. And here’s another one: El-Sayed turned out a lot of voters. The last time Michigan Democrats had a semi-competitive primary was in 2024. Elissa Slotkin romped with 76 percent of 934,000 votes. More than 1.5 million people voted in yesterday’s primary. In a primary race in a state where the total number of eligible voters—of both parties—is around 8 million, that’s a lot of excitement; a lot of energy. You have to give El-Sayed credit for a lot of it. El-Sayed dramatically underperformed his polls. The last batch of polls had El-Sayed ahead by +13 on average. His worst poll in the final days had him at +8. As of this writing, he’s ahead by just about 1 percent. Also concerning is the voting pattern. This race had become a referendum on El-Sayed. He was the main character. He was so far ahead and had so much energy behind his campaign that the question for Democrats wasn’t so much Stevens vs. El-Sayed, but, “Are you sure you want to roll with this guy?” When Slotkin beat Mike Rogers in 2024, she won by a total of 19,000 votes out of 5.6 million votes cast. How did she do it? She rolled up huge margins in Wayne, Washtenaw, and Ingham Counties where she won with Saddam numbers. She dominated 8 of the 11 most populous counties. But she also hung on in the rural counties. Slotkin only dropped below 30 percent in a handful of rural outposts. The difference between hitting 30 percent, or falling to 20 percent, in a county with 5,000 voters isn’t much—500 votes. But again: She won by 19,000 votes, total. And there are a lot of those small, rural counties. So the blueprint for a Democrat winning Michigan is: Absolutely crush with the black vote in Wayne, Oakland, and other dense urban counties, but also . . . Find every vote you can in the small, rural counties. Lose by 30 points, not 40 points. Look at that list up top 👆. El-Sayed lost Wayne and Oakland by >6 points. This tells us that he wasn’t able to excite the African-American voters who are the foundation of the party in Michigan. (Our Jonathan Cohn had his eye on this possibility, and wrote about it last week.) Now maybe El-Sayed turns out those voters in November. But remember: He doesn’t just need huge turnout in those counties—he needs to absolutely crush the margins. I am slightly concerned with El-Sayed’s numbers in Macomb, too. Macomb is an affluent white Detroit suburb where Mike Rogers did very well in 2024. El-Sayed lost Macomb by 7 points. He’s going to need to get a bunch of votes out of there and probably can’t afford to lose Macomb by >10 points. On the rural counties, it’s a mixed bag for El-Sayed. He did well in places like Iron and Marquette Counties while Stevens won most of the rural counties. But El-Sayed stayed competitive. He didn’t dip below the 30 percent mark anywhere. This suggests to me that rural Democrats are not totally opposed to him. They’ll listen to his pitch and if he connects, then maybe he can get the numbers he needs from the hinterlands. The final concern for El-Sayed is that Mike Rogers has done this before. Democrats are dismissive of Rogers as a carpetbagging empty suit. Fair enough. But Rogers ran statewide two years ago and earned a lot of votes. He’s been tested in a high-profile, big-time campaign. There won’t be any bombshells blowing him up. Two years ago he got 48.3 percent of the vote against a quality Democrat. The guy has already convinced 2.7 million Michiganders to pull the lever for him once. In 2018, Republican John James ran for Debbie Stabenow’s Senate seat. He got 45.76 percent of the vote—good enough for 1.9 million votes. Encouraged by this showing, James ran it back in 2020 for the other Michigan Senate seat. He ticked up to 48.22 percent and 2.6 million votes. This isn’t straight apples-to-apples. But it’s close. It’s hard to picture Rogers doing much worse in 2026 than he did in 2024. Without Trump at the top of the ticket, he could lose some altitude. But he probably has a hard floor of 47 percent. Do you like deep-dive analysis that has a point of view but doesn’t pander to your preferences? That’s what we do here, every day. Come ride with us: Bottom line: We have a bunch of conflicting signals here. This should be a winnable seat for Democrats in a very good environment. But he also has work to do, especially with African-American voters. Mike Rogers may not be the tomato-can people expect. And the race might turn out to be a close-run thing, determined by less than 50,000 votes. All in all, I like his chances; but it isn’t a gimme. Last thing: Another hidden advantage for El-Sayed is that Francesca Hong is going to act as a human shield for his campaign. Every time the media has a “Look at the radical DSA” story, it’ll focus on Hong and El-Sayed will seem mainstream by comparison. The era of drone warfare is already posing risks to civilian aviation. Yikes. This past May, a twin-engine Beechcraft King Air medevac plane took off from Roswell, New Mexico, and headed west to the town of Ruidoso to pick up a patient. It shouldn’t have been a challenging flight for the two pilots and two nurses aboard. The temperature was 69 degrees; the sky was clear. The 60-mile journey normally takes a half hour, at most. But once airborne, the plane ran into trouble. At the White Sands Missile Range that night, US military personnel were conducting a GPS jamming exercise that left the King Air pilots—and anyone else within hundreds of miles—unable to use modern navigation systems. Forced to revert to older technology, ones that they rarely if ever use, the medevac pilots got disoriented and crashed into the side of a mountain. There were no survivors. The accident marked the first time that GPS jamming had contributed to the crash of a civilian plane in the United States. But it was just one of a string of recent disruptions across the world. The skies are more contested than ever, whether it’s civilian drones wandering out of the approved zone or US agencies getting their signals crossed, as happened earlier this year when New Mexico and Texas scared the public by temporarily closing their airspace. (It turned out that US Customs and Border Patrol were using anti-drone lasers in that area.) The GPS jamming exercise that led to this latest crash is not a singular event. In the past year, the US military appeared to have sent out notices for at least 10 such exercises. “As drone warfare and electronic warfare expand, airlines are increasingly encountering navigation disruptions hundreds of miles beyond the actual conflict zone,” says Eliran Almog, CEO of the cybersecurity firm Cyviation. I’m extrapolating out to the end of Gretchen Whitmer’s term in 2027. This may sound cruel, but Stevens strikes me as the living embodiment of a replacement-level Democrat. I’m going to openly say what we only ever gesture at; I’m always made deeply uncomfortable by the subtext of these conversations; same with Mamdani. There is a large portion of the American population that does not want to treat Muslims as full citizens of the American country with the same rights and the same responsibilities as anyone else in the country. And whenever we talk about “is $Muslim a good politician?” - well, we need to talk about that, obviously, the stakes are too high to not do that - but I always feel like we concede a bit too much ground by refusing to attack the premise that Mamdani and El-Sayed have as much right to participate in society as anyone else. This is important enough to me that I always feel… uncomfortable. These are important questions. But it’s important that we maintain the answer to the question that these articles only ever gesture at - “is it acceptable for a politician to be a Muslim?” with “screw you, of course it is.” JVL, I really appreciate your perspective on Michigan. I understand why so many of us are anxious. El-Sayed is an unconventional candidate who won a close primary, and there are legitimate questions about whether some Michigan voters will respond to his outsider status. Those concerns are real. At the same time, I keep coming back to the thought that what Democrats have been doing for the last several election cycles hasn't consistently produced the results we want. If we're serious about building a durable majority, perhaps we need to be willing to take some calculated risks instead of defaulting to the traditional "safe" or "moderate"playbook. That doesn't mean there aren't risks here. There clearly are. But every new political direction begins as an experiment. If the party is going to adapt to where the electorate may be heading rather than where it has been, this may be one of those moments. Like you, I'm choosing cautious optimism and hoping El-Sayed can put together the coalition needed to defeat Mike Rogers. Emergency Triad: The United States commits imperial suicide. title: Cadillac Might Actually Build A Hypercar To Challenge McLaren And Ferrari - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update Cadillac is increasingly getting serious about motorsports, with entries in Formula One and the top tier of the FIA World Endurance Championship. The automaker is now teasing that some of its track-proven know-how is coming to a future vehicle. The machine apparently takes inspiration from the V-Series.R race car, but isn't necessarily something designed for the track. We won't have long to ponder the mystery at least, as it's slated for a debut during Monterey Car Week. Cadillac isn't telling us much about what it's bringing to Monterey. In a social media post to Instagram, the company describes it as "a showcase of what happens when track-proven engineering becomes future luxury." The accompanying image shows a portion of the V-Series.R. The Quail Motorsports Gathering is one of the premier events during Monterey Car Week. The event focuses on classic, new, and future performance vehicles, in addition to concepts. For example, in 2025, the Lexus Sport Concept debuted there, and Pagani displayed its final Zonda. Cadillac was there in 2025 with the Elevated Velocity Concept that imagined a rugged electric SUV, with a fresh take on the styling language from its existing EVs. Given the image of the V-Series.R, the reference to "the track," and the statement about becoming "future luxury," we are wondering whether Cadillac is bringing a high-performance, circuit-focused machine to the show, with the intention of putting it into production. A possibility is that the brand could sell a version of the V-Series.R to a handful of ultra-wealthy clients. The idea of such a project isn't without precedent, with several automakers selling versions of their endurance racers. For example, Aston Martin built the Valkyrie LM, and the Ferrari 499P Modificata also followed this recipe. McLaren let folks drive the Le Mans Hypercar as part of its Project: Endurance. These initiatives allow a brand's most dedicated fans to experience just a little of what it's like to be a racing driver at the elite level. When behind the wheel of a V-Series.R, the driver would experience a hybrid-assisted, naturally aspirated 5.5-liter V8. In competition specification, the rules limit the output to 670 horsepower. A seven-speed sequential gearbox sends the power to the rear wheels. Some automakers that offer versions of their race cars to customers increase engine output because, while these are track-only machines, they aren't meant for actual competition in a given series. By not having any rules to adhere to, the engineers can push the powertrain even harder. Another possibility is that Cadillac could go even further and create a road-going hypercar based on the V-Series.R. However, building a few more examples of an existing race car is a far less complicated project than certifying a production vehicle for sale. There are emissions and safety standards that must be met for the vehicle to be road-legal. However, Cadillac has teased this possibility. In 2024, Michael Simcoe, the senior vice president of GM Global Design at the time, commented about the possibility of Caddy getting a hypercar: "Could we build one? Yes. Would we like to? Yes. Are we building one? That would be giving too much away." While that statement was from years ago, these projects take time to develop. If Cadillac builds a road-going hypercar, the burning question would be how to differentiate it from the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X, which seems to fill the same space. The Chevy is a mid-engined, track-focused supercar with a combination of a twin-turbocharged 5.5-liter V8 and a front-mounted electric motor to make a total of 1,250 horsepower, with all-wheel drive. The existing Corvette Z06 already shares some attributes with the V-Series.R by using a naturally aspirated 5.5-liter V8. In the Chevy, it makes 670 horsepower at 8,400 rpm and can get the car to 60 mph in 2.6 seconds. In a theoretical road-going V-Series.R, the addition of hybrid assistance would provide a slight power boost, potentially putting its output between the Z06 and ZR1X. Teasers like this are fun because there's real mystery around them. We don't have spy shots of Cadillac developing a hypercar, and there aren't any trustworthy rumors that the automaker has one ready to debut. But the company has clearly kept something a secret. In an ideal world, we'd love to finally see a Cadillac hypercar that fulfills the promise of concepts such as the Cien or the Opulent Velocity. However, it's probably better to be more realistic. The easier solution is to offer the V-Series.R as a track car. We can't wait to see what Cadillac is doing. Whatever Cadillac is cooking up, it will be revealed on August 14 at The Quail Motorsports Gathering. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. While I like the idea of a Caddy Hypercar, a version of the Celestiq with the Corvette ZR1X 5.5l hybrid v8 would make for THAT flagship vehicle the brand deserves.  Put some of the F1 tech and high power in more high-end Cadillac production vehicles very much the way theyve pushed forward with the CT5V Blackwing.  That car has tons of street credibility. Nice cherry-picking the F1 results from their first year starting from scratch, while conveniently ignoring their decade of dominance in IMSA. title: V Corps welcomes Command Sgt. Maj. Bohannon as their senior enlisted leader - army.mil
content: POZNAŃ, Poland — Incoming Command Sgt. Maj. Eric S. Bohannon assumes responsibility as the V Corps senior enlisted leader as the corps’ colors pass from one set of trusted hands to another during a ceremony at Camp Kościuszko, July 31, 2026. Bohannon succeeds Command Sgt. Maj. Phillip B. Blaisdell, after Blaisdell’s three years as the V Corps command sergeant major and 34 years of active-duty service. The passing of the colors is the heart of the ceremony and symbolizes the transfer of responsibility for the corp’s Soldiers. The colors represent the organization’s history and traditions. The physical transfer of the flag demonstrates the command’s trust in Bohannon to lead and care for the formation. V Corps Commander, Lt. Gen. Charles D. Costanza, who presided over the ceremony, described the transition as both a farewell to a trusted leader and the return of a familiar member of the V Corps team. During his remarks, Costanza credited Blaisdell with being a constant presence along the European eastern flank. “You have been the backbone of this organization,” Costanza said. “You have been the voice of our Soldiers. You ensured that our formations remained ready, disciplined and prepared to deter aggression.” Blaisdell assumed responsibility as the V Corps command sergeant major in August 2023 and advised the commander on matters affecting Soldiers. He traveled Europe’s eastern flank to observe training, visit living areas and speak directly with Soldiers and leaders. In his farewell remarks, Blaisdell thanked his family, fellow leaders, Soldiers and allied partners who supported him throughout his career. He then challenged V Corps noncommissioned officers (NCOs) to continue enforcing standards, developing Soldiers and preparing their formations for future conflict. “We are the envy of the world, the noncommissioned officer corps,” Blaisdell said. “Every army in the world wants what we have. We have it because our commanders trust us.” Blaisdell reminded NCOs that the trust placed in them carries a duty to care for Soldiers and families while ensuring their formations remain ready. “That’s our responsibility,” Blaisdell said. “It’s a sacred trust”. He also took a moment to reflect on the personal cost of military service and the impact it can have on family members who supported him throughout more than three decades in uniform. “I’m satisfied that I’ve given everything for the Army,” Blaisdell said. “I’m ready to be Phil from Florida, and I’m ready to be a better son, a better husband, a better father and a better grandfather.” As Blaisdell’s remarks reached their conclusion, Bohannon picks up the torch, ready to continue where Blaisdell leaves off. Having previously served as the V Corps Forward command sergeant major, Bohannon returns with expertise across the corps’ European operations and partnerships. “Eric, your experience here in Europe at the tactical level, the installation level and the operational level makes you exactly the right person to be here and take over this corps,” Costanza said. Bohannon thanked Costanza for the opportunity to return to V Corps and praised Blaisdell as a warfighter, mentor and friend whose influence would remain within the organization. “Your spirit will live on in this corps for quite a while,” Bohannon said to Blaisdell. “You’re a brother. You’re a lifelong friend. You’re a member of this corps for life.” Bohannon pledged to work alongside V Corps leaders and allied partners while keeping the corps focused on its mission in Europe. “I promise to be a great teammate, and I look forward to continuing to work with you all as we lead and prepare our formations for combat,” Bohannon said. Bohannon then challenged V Corps Soldiers to understand the purpose behind their presence on Europe’s eastern flank and to maintain the readiness required to respond during a crisis. “We’re not leaving, not under my watch,” Bohannon said. “Make sure your formations are the most trained, the most fit, the most lethal and the most disciplined. We’ll always be ready to respond and, if necessary, fight and win.” The ceremony concluded with the Victory March and the Army Song, beginning a new chapter in the corps’ senior enlisted leadership. “Victory 7 signing on,” Bohannon said. “It will be done.” V Corps transfers responsibility to Command Sgt. title: KRK announces new V Series Five studio monitors - DJ Mag
content: The fifth generation of the flagship studio monitors KRK has announced a new collection of its flagship V Series studio monitors. The fifth-generation units add new wireless control capabilities that incorporate KRK Mesh technology, meaning you can control the monitors remotely on your phone via the KRK Control App. They promise to set "a new benchmark for the performance, innovation, and sonic accuracy that define the KRK name". There are three new units, comprising three units: the V4, which features a four-inch woofer, the V6, which incorporates a 6.5-inch woofer, and the V8, which has an eight-inch woofer. All three units are built with custom Kevlar woofers and encased in low-distortion cast aluminium frames. The Nashville-based company — which is part of Gibson — first teased the new V Series Five collection back in January. The KRK V Series was first launched in 1997. In 2024, KRK also released the fifth generation of its popular ROKIT range of monitor speakers, available again in three sizes: five-inch, seven-inch and eight-inch cones. The ROKIT speakers were made into a LEGO version by Hungarian designer Tamás Borján in 2024.

title: TDK releases 125 V axial aluminum electrolytic capacitors for DC-link banks - Charged EVs
content:
Posted August 5, 2026 by Chris Ruoff & filed under Newswire, The Tech. TDK has added 125 V-rated components to its B43693/B43793 axial-lead and soldering star aluminum electrolytic capacitor series, and upgraded the 63 V range of its existing B41687/B41787 series. The parts are intended for DC-link capacitor banks in systems running from 48 V up to 120 V: small xEVs, micromobility platforms, forklifts, electric boats and humanoid robots. The B43693/B43793 series spans 125 V to 250 V, handles ripple currents up to 21.6 A and operates at temperatures up to +140° C. Capacitance runs from 56 µF to 650 µF in can sizes from 16 x 25 mm to 21 x 49 mm (diameter x length), and both series are rated for a useful life of 2,500 h at ambient temperatures up to +125° C. TDK says the 125 V variant is generally used for 96 V system designs that are constrained on space, exposed to high thermal stress and subject to dynamic load conditions requiring stable energy buffering. The upgraded B41687/B41787 series covers 25 V to 63 V and shares the same axial-lead and soldering star construction, which standardizes design across voltage classes. Those parts operate at up to +150° C and offer capacitance from 510 µF to 4,800 µF. Supporting a higher DC-link voltage in a single component removes the need to connect capacitors in series, which TDK says can simplify capacitor-bank design and improve system robustness and efficiency. Series-connected electrolytics normally need voltage-balancing resistors across each capacitor to keep the string’s voltage evenly divided. TDK characterizes all four series by low equivalent series resistance (ESR) and high ripple current capability, which it says reduces power losses and improves thermal efficiency in the DC-link stage of an inverter. Vibration resistance is rated at up to 20 g as standard, and up to 60 g is available on request. The axial-lead and soldering star terminals allow horizontal or vertical mounting on PCBs and busbars. Mounting the 125 V parts of the B43693/B43793 series to a heat sink more than doubles their rated ripple current, which TDK says lets designers use fewer capacitors per bank and cut assembly costs. The specified ripple current of an 18 x 30 mm component rises from 5.2 A at +105° C ambient to 11.1 A when the aluminum case is held at +105° C by a heat sink. title: Maserati’s V-8 Could Be Coming Back If Customer Demand Builds, Exec Says - Road & Track
content: The GranTurismo, GranCabrio, and even the Grecale could potentially fit a V-8, though the company’s engineering boss says the appeal is more emotional than performance-driven. These days, V-8 engines are making a triumphant stand amongst the world of American performance vehicles amid regulatory rollbacks — and it seems as if the Europeans don't want to be left out of the fun. Despite spending years touting the benefits of its (admittedly lovely) Nettuno twin-turbo V-6, Maserati is reportedly mulling over the idea of bringing back a proper eight-cylinder powertrain in select models. The news comes by way of Australia's CarSales, which recently sat down to interview Maserati head of engineering Davide Danesin. Upon being pressed about the brand’s opinion on the future of V-8 powertrains, Danesin noted that there is, perhaps unsurprisingly, some customer demand for such a project. Furthermore, he noted that some of the brand’s existing platforms could potentially accept a V-8 engine, as the GranTurismo/GranCabrio and Grecale were designed from the jump to accommodate different powerplants. And while the executive didn’t go as far as to confirm the existence of a V-8 model in the works, he made his personal feelings on the matter pretty clear. “My personal opinion is yes: I think the V-8 could potentially be coming back... I’m sure that if we would be making it, we would be selling it [but] maybe not in big numbers,” Danesin told CarSales. “We believe that a good V-8 engine could fit... it looks like the momentum for V-8 is building up,” he added. “The decision to make it is very much depending on company strategies [but] I think potentially the space is there.” The GranTurismo and GranCabrio would be the most natural landing spots for a V-8 engine, with the last-gen models’ identity wrapped up in their Ferrari-derived motors; a V-8-powered Grecale crossover seems less likely, though such a move could make it a more compelling alternative to Mercedes-AMG and BMW M rivals. That said, Danesin doesn’t believe a V-8 would offer a transformative change in terms of the performance, noting how stout the current V-6 is in every respect. Instead, he believes the desire for more cylinders comes from an emotional standpoint.“I think the need of a V-8 is [about] having the proper engine for a certain vehicle,” Danesin told CarSales. “It is more a perception issue.” It’s unclear what a new V-8 from Maserati could look like, but given the market, we’d expect a set of turbos to be involved. Don’t expect any electrification, however, as Danesin said he doesn’t believe in the concept for Maserati vehicles; the brand would rather keep the identities of its various powertrains distinct from one another, which is a bold choice if nothing else. Nancy Virginia (McKean) Gerber, age 78, of Butler, Indiana, passed away peacefully on July 30, 2026, at Auburn Village with her daughter by her side. Nancy was born in Auburn, Indiana, on August 27, 1947, to the late George and Virginia (Whitbey) McKean. She married her high school sweetheart, Robert "Gerb" Gerber on December 24, 1966 who preceded her in death August 13, 2019. Nancy graduated from Eastside High School in 1966. In her earlier years, she worked at Pizza Hut in Auburn, among other places. She retired from GE in 2008. Nancy loved her community and volunteered her time for community events throughout the years. Nancy never met a stranger and had a remarkable gift for making everyone feel welcome. She touched the lives of many with her warm heart and generous spirit. She was an avid supporter of Eastside sports. You could often find her on the sidelines of boys and girls basketball games cheering on the Blazers. She took great joy in watching young people learn, grow, and succeed, especially Madison, Cade and Owen and their friends. Her enthusiasm, encouragement, and support will be remembered for years to come. During her time at Auburn Village, she found a love for painting and bingo. title: Chelsea v Juventus | Match | Official Site - Chelsea Football Club
content: There were first outings in blue for Mike Penders, Geovany Quenda and Danny Welbeck, plus the return to action of Mykhailo Mudryk, as our pre-season campaign continued with a narrow defeat to Juventus. Quenda and Welbeck were in from the start in Hong Kong, and both were sharp in the opening 45 minutes. However, with few chances fashioned by either side, the game was goalless at the interval In the second period, moments after several substitutions were made by Xabi Alonso, Juventus winger Edon Zhegrova produced a fine left-footed strike to beat half-time substitute Penders. We pushed hard in search of an equaliser in the time that remained – with Mudryk playing the final eight minutes – but couldn't level the contest despite late opportunities for Estevao Willian and Romeo Lavia. Alonso included two of our summer arrivals in his starting XI. Robert Sanchez returned from injury in goal and was protected by a back four of Marco Palestra, Wesley Fofana, Tosin Adarabiyo and Jorrel Hato. Moises Caicedo was given his first minutes of pre-season and captained the side. He was deployed in midfield alongside 16-year-old Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, while the attack included Quenda, Joao Pedro, Jamie Gittens and Welbeck. There were few chances of note for either side in the opening 20 minutes. An early shot from Andrea Cambiaso was blocked well by Tosin and midfielder Manuel Locatelli drove an effort wide from distance. Quenda was a lively presence on his first start and dovetailed well with Palestra down the Chelsea right. The Portuguese winger fashioned our first sight of goal with a whipped cross that Joao Pedro glanced wide, before he drilled an effort from the edge of the box over. Juventus' threat predominantly came on the counter, as when the Blues had possession the Italian side sat deep in their own defensive third. Fabio Miretti did cause a moment of panic for the Blues with a poked attempt from a Cambiaso cross, but Sanchez had it covered. Welbeck linked well with his new team-mates and Quenda was a threat moving inside off the right. The 19-year-old fashioned room for a shot and powered an effort toward goal, only for a Juventus defender to stand firm and block. As the opening 45 minutes approached its conclusion, Sanchez was tested. Jeremie Boga, schooled in our Academy, was given room to drive an effort at goal, and the Blues stopper lept to his left to save. Arkadiusz Milik then fired wide for the Serie A side. Alonso made four alterations at the break. Penders replaced Sanchez, Mamdou Sarr stepped on for Tosin, Estevao was introduced for Quenda and Nicolas Jackson came on for Welbeck. Jackson was immediately involved, producing a surging run that saw him burst beyond two challenges and slip a pass through to Palestra, whose attempt was blocked en route to goal. The Italian did force a save from Mattia Perin soon after, as he raced onto an excellent Caicedo pass and tried to guide an attempt beyond the Juventus goalkeeper. Perin reacted well to save, and then got to the rebound before Gittens. Shortly after the hour mark, Alonso turned to his bench. Josh Acheampong, Tayo Subuloye, Aaron Anselmino, Dario Essugo, Romeo Lavia, Dastan Satpayev and Liam Delap were brought on, with Palestra, Fofana, Hato, Caicedo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens and Joao Pedro replaced. From the restart, Juventus broke the deadlock. It was a fine strike. The ball was knocked to Zhegrova on the edge of the Chelsea penalty area and he whipped a fine strike into the top corner. As those introduced settled into the contest, we began to take control of possession. Juventus continued to defend well, although our threat increased in the final ten minutes. In the closing stages, there was the return of Mudryk, who replaced Jackson. It was the first time the Ukraine international was in action for the Blues since November 2024. Alonso's side pushed for an equaliser. Estevao rasped a free-kick into the arms of Perin before Anselmino also forced a save from the goalkeeper. The final action of the game saw a passage of Chelsea possession end with a pass into the feet of Lavia 20 yards from goal. The Belgian curled a shot toward the top corner, but his attempt cleared the crossbar and the Blues were beaten. The next stop on our summer tour takes the Blues to Indonesia. We will face AC Milan at Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta on Saturday. On 30 July 2026, the High Court handed down its judgment in Competition and Markets Authority v Emma Matratzen GmbH & Others. As discussed in our earlier article, the case centred on Emma Sleep's use of "was/now" pricing and whether Emma Sleep should be subject to the Competition and Markets Authority’s (CMA) proposed 1:2 fixed volume requirement (FVR). A 1:2 FVR would mean that for every two products offered for sale at the lower price, Emma Sleep would need to sell, or have sold, one product at the higher reference price. The Court declined to endorse the CMA's proposed 1:2 FVR and rejected the CMA’s broader argument that low sales volumes at a reference price are, by themselves, sufficient to establish that a reference price is misleading. The Court has now asked the CMA and Emma Sleep to work together to identify an alternative Order that does not include a 1:2 FVR. The CMA wished to secure an enforcement order requiring Emma Sleep to comply with a 1:2 FVR, which was already enshrined in its online mattresses reference pricing guidance (and which the CMA reserved the right to apply in other sectors). The Court declined to impose such a requirement, finding that a failure to satisfy a fixed ratio would not necessarily mean that consumer law had been breached.  The CMA has subsequently withdrawn its controversial online mattresses reference pricing guidance. This is likely to prompt a rethink in terms of how any future CMA guidance deals with this issue. The Court accepted that the proportion of products sold at the higher reference price is relevant when assessing whether a pricing claim is misleading. However, it rejected the CMA's argument that low sales volumes alone demonstrate that a reference price is not genuine or realistic. The Court adopted a broader, more fact-specific assessment, holding that the analysis must take account of all relevant circumstances rather than relying on a single numerical threshold. A recurring theme throughout the judgment is consumer purchasing behaviour. The Court accepted evidence that mattresses are relatively expensive, infrequent and generally non-urgent purchases, meaning consumers may actively wait for promotions before deciding to buy. A consumer purchasing a mattress reduced to £750 from £1,000 after several weeks would still consider £750 a good deal, even if no mattresses had been sold at the higher price, because the consumer had seen the previous price and chosen to wait. The Court concluded that the fact many consumers purchase during promotional periods does not automatically mean that the higher reference price was unrealistic or misleading. The Court did, however, flag that if "many weeks later" the same reference price continued to be used, consumers might begin to doubt whether it was genuine. The judgment therefore reinforces the importance of analysing how consumers are likely to behave in a particular market, and the duration for which a reference price has been maintained, when assessing pricing claims. The Court also took into account what it saw as Emma Sleep's genuine belief that the reference price represented a realistic selling price. The Court held that an average consumer would regard it as relevant whether a trader genuinely believed that products could be sold at the stated reference price. Importantly, the Court clarified that a trader's subjective beliefs alone would not be conclusive, but that where those beliefs were also objectively reasonable, this would support the case that the reference price was genuine and not misleading. While the Court stopped short of creating a formal legal test based on subjective belief, it concluded that the CMA's approach placed insufficient weight on wider contextual factors, including the trader's own assessment of its pricing, that may be relevant when assessing whether a reference price is genuine or realistic. Another important theme running through the judgment is proportionality. The Court expressed concern that imposing a rigid FVR could expose Emma Sleep to what it described as "draconian consequences" in circumstances where no underlying consumer law infringement had occurred. The Court also observed that it would be disproportionate to require Emma Sleep to run the risk of a potentially significant decline in its business fortunes given the concerns identified with the proposed 1:2 FVR. Emma Sleep had argued that the CMA was forcing it to abandon its approach of running regular seasonal discounts in favour of an "everyday low prices" strategy. As noted above, following the judgment, the CMA has temporarily withdrawn its online mattress sale guidance. It remains to be seen if the guidance will be reinstated or if more nuanced guidance will be published following the Court’s refusal to endorse a 1:2 FVR. However, it is worth noting that the High Court judgment remains largely consistent with the principle-based CTSI Guidance on Pricing Practices. The CTSI Guidance has always been clear that sales volumes at the reference price is just one of many factors that influence whether a reference price is "genuine" or not. The CTSI's approach has arguably been vindicated by the High Court decision. On the whole, the judgment indicates that courts may favour a fact-specific assessment rather than reliance on rigid numerical thresholds. In some cases, economic evidence may be required to show how consumers respond to discounts in different sectors. Businesses should therefore continue to assess reference pricing holistically, considering factors such as pricing history, duration, sales data, commercial rationale and the expectations of the average consumer. The judgment does not bring the Emma Sleep litigation to an end. While the Court declined to impose the CMA's proposed 1:2 FVR, it found that Emma Sleep had committed several admitted infringements and invited the parties to seek agreement on the terms of a revised enforcement order. If agreement cannot be reached, further submissions will be heard in Autumn 2026. Notwithstanding the defeat for the CMA in this case, misleading pricing practices remain a key focus in the CMA's enforcement agenda. This judgment, which relates to a case brought under the pre-Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (DMCCA) regime, will no doubt give the CMA reason to reflect, but it is unlikely to dampen its enthusiasm for bringing future reference pricing cases. It is also important to note that in DMCCA enforcement cases, the CMA has the power to impose retrospective penalties without needing to specify any formula (FVR or otherwise) governing future conduct. It will only need to determine whether the reference pricing practice in question constituted an unfair commercial practice for the purposes of Part 4 of the DMCCA. Note: On 22 May 2026, the High Court imposed a separate order on Emma Sleep in respect of its wider promotional practices, including urgency and scarcity claims. title: Springboks team v Argentina: Winners and losers as 'South Africa's golden boy' is back and 'unlucky trio' miss out - Planet Rugby
content: Springboks fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and front-row Wilco Louw (inset). Following the announcement of the Springboks team to face Argentina at Estadio Jose Amalfitani in Buenos Aires, here are our winners and losers from Rassie Erasmus’ selections. After cruising to impressive Nations Championship victories over England, Scotland and Wales last month, Erasmus opted to leave several players behind in South Africa for this clash with Los Pumas. The Boks head coach has made 13 changes to his starting line-up with scrum-half Cobus Reinach and full-back Aphelele Fassi being the only survivors from the run-on side which beat Wales in Durban last month. So, without further ado, we unpack the Springboks team for this eagerly anticipated international and pick out our winners and losers. The Toshiba Brave Lupus-bound full-back will wear the Springboks’ number 15 jersey for the third successive match after also starting in those triumphs against Scotland and Wales. Fassi has endured an injury-hit season, and while he put in a solid showing in the Springboks’ 42-28 victory over Scotland, he delivered an underwhelming performance during their one-sided 43-0 triumph against Wales the following week. Although he showed flashes of brilliance, his game was littered with unforced errors, and he can consider himself lucky to start ahead of Quan Horn. Van der Merwe and Moodie have had limited opportunities to show off their wares for South Africa at Test level, with the latter last seeing action for a meagre 12 minutes when he came off the replacements bench during the Boks’ 45-21 win over England. Although Moodie is primarily a wing, he is also adept at outside centre and will wear the number 13 jersey as part of a solid-looking midfield alongside Andre Esterhuizen against Argentina. Meanwhile, Van der Merwe was in action for the full 80 minutes against Scotland, but despite impressing under the high ball and on defence, he had few attacking opportunities and will be keen to improve in that department against Argentina. Esterhuizen and Hooker’s absence in the Springboks set-up during the Nations Championship was due to fitness issues, with the former seeing just 10 minutes of action in the clash against England before being forced off the field with a fractured cheekbone. He returns to action in his favoured inside centre role to form an exciting midfield partnership with Moodie, although the Sharks star’s versatility could see him moving to the flank later in the game against Argentina. Hooker also returns to action after he left the field due to concussion early in the second half of their victory against Scotland. That match was the left winger’s first match back since recovering from a shoulder injury, which he sustained while on duty for the Sharks against the Ospreys in April, and he will be highly motivated to hit the ground running this weekend. There is plenty of excitement in the Springboks ranks as the golden boy of South African rugby makes his long-awaited return to action after being sidelined with an ankle injury, which he sustained while on duty for the Stormers in a United Rugby Championship (URC) quarter-final against Cardiff at the end of May. Although the likes of Manie Libbok, Handre Pollard and Vusi Moyo impressed while calling the shots as the Boks’ chief playmakers in the Nations Championship, Feinberg-Mngomezulu is their first-choice fly-half and his performance against Los Pumas will be closely scrutinised ahead of the Boks’ eagerly anticipated Greatest Rivalry series with their arch-rivals, the All Blacks. After initially being named to captain the Springboks during their Nations Championship opener against England in Johannesburg last month, the experienced loose forward was forced to withdraw on the day of that match due to a hamstring strain. That injury also kept him on the sidelines for the subsequent matches against Scotland and Wales and, in his absence, rookie flanker Paul de Villiers did a more than adequate job as his replacement. There was even talk in some quarters of De Villiers replacing Kolisi permanently as the world champions’ first choice openside flanker. However, Erasmus dismissed such claims when asked last week whether Kolisi would captain the team in the series against the All Blacks, by stating: “Without a doubt. He is fit, he is the captain.” The 35-year-old now gets the opportunity to repay the faith which his coach has in him. The return to action of the experienced second-row combination of Eben Etzebeth and Lood de Jager will be a shot in the arm for the Springboks, particularly with the Greatest Rivalry series against New Zealand looming large on the horizon. Etzebeth missed South Africa’s Nations Championship matches due to his latest concussion, while De Jager has had a plethora of injuries in recent years, the latest of which was a hip surgery setback from earlier in 2026. Ruan Nortje was a regular starter in the Boks’ second-row during the Nations Championship while the likes of Etzebeth, De Jager, RG Snyman, Jean Kleyn and Salmaan Moerat were all sidelined with injuries. That meant South Africa’s lock cupboard was bare, but with the former duo ruled fit to face Argentina, there is suddenly much more optimism about the Boks’ second-row stocks. If Etzebeth and De Jager come through the Argentina clash unscathed, there will be more confidence in the world champions’ ranks ahead of the Greatest Rivalry Tests. After Evan Roos was dropped from the Boks squad, and Jasper Wiese among the group who were left behind in South Africa, Hanekom was the favourite to start at number eight in this fixture, and that’s exactly what happened. After starting on the blindside flank against England last month, Hanekom has not had a look-in for the Boks again, and a barnstorming game against Argentina should put some pressure on Jasper Wiese for the green and gold number eight jersey for the first Test against the All Blacks in Johannesburg later this month. Meanwhile, with Pieter-Steph du Toit firmly entrenched as the world champions’ first-choice blindside flanker and arguably the best player in that position in the world, it was either Louw or Ben-Jason Dixon who was going to wear the Boks’ number seven jersey for this clash while the two-time World Rugby Player of the Year is among the group of players who stayed behind in Johannesburg. Springboks team: Five takeaways as Rassie Erasmus braced for All Blacks selection dilemmas with injury ‘crisis’ easing Louw was initially a surprise omission when Erasmus named his Rugby Championship squad but was called up to that group as additional forward cover in the build-up to their first Test against England. He made one appearance off the bench against Scotland and gave a good account of himself, and will be keen to build on that effort against Argentina. After last playing for the Springboks in their Nations Championship opener against England, the 31-year-old front-row returns to the world champions’ starting line-up for this fixture. He gets the nod as the starting tighthead prop, with Zachary Porthen named as his back-up on the bench while Wilco Louw misses out on the matchday squad. Du Toit, who is also able to play on the loosehead side of the scrum, started five of the Springboks’ six Rugby Championship matches in 2025 and was also in the number three jersey in the November internationals against France and Ireland. That experience will come in handy against Los Pumas this weekend. With Cobus Reinach getting the nod as the starting scrum-half and set to resume his halfback partnership with Stormers team-mate Feinberg-Mngomezulu in the Test arena, it was down to Van den Berg and Herschel Jantjies for the replacement slot. Van den Berg got the nod, and if he comes onto the field against Los Pumas, it will be the first time he sees action since sustaining a serious bicep injury while on URC duty for the Lions at the end of May. Prior to that, the 28-year-old had won a handful of caps for the Boks and shone for the Lions at club level. He will be determined to continue in that vein in Buenos Aires. With just 26 players named in the Springboks’ travelling squad, Lions utility player Horn is part of the unlucky trio who miss out on selection for the matchday squad, and he can consider himself unlucky. Although primarily a full-back, Horn was a shock selection to start at fly-half for the Boks’ Nations Championship warm-up clash against the Barbarians and, although he did not set the world alight, he put in a solid performance. He delivered a similar showing when he came off the bench to play in that position against Scotland but finished that match in his favoured full-back role and also performed adequately. Horn came into this Argentina game in direct competition with Fassi for the starting full-back role and with the latter receiving the nod, he can consider himself unlucky to miss out on selection as one of the replacements. It’s a similar story for experienced Bayonne scrum-half Jantjies, who misses out on selection for the matchday squad with Van den Berg preferred to him as Reinach’s deputy in Buenos Aires. After last representing South Africa in a Rugby Championship Test against Argentina in the build-up to the 2023 Rugby World Cup in France, Jantjies was a surprise inclusion in Erasmus’ Nations Championship squad earlier this year. He impressed off the bench during a one-sided 43-0 triumph against Wales and will be disappointed to have missed out on selection for the Argentina encounter. The Stormers-bound tighthead prop is the third unlucky player to miss out on selection, with Thomas du Toit being named to start this weekend while Porthen has been preferred to do the job off the replacements bench. While Louw is arguably the most powerful scrummager of that trio, Du Toit and Porthen have proven to be better ball players than him, and that seems to have counted against the burly 32-year-old. Louw was involved in the Boks’ Nations Championship triumphs over Scotland and Wales as he started in the former clash and came off the bench during the latter. However, his services will not be required in Buenos Aires on Saturday. While he will be happy to be in the matchday squad, the versatile Bulls forward can feel somewhat aggrieved to be lining up amongst the replacements again after he also played off the bench in the recent matches against England and Wales while missing out on selection against Scotland. When Kolisi withdrew in the build-up to that England game, Van Staden, who has been the Boks skipper’s deputy for the openside flanker position in recent years, was overlooked with young Stormers tearaway De Villiers preferred to step into the starting role. And now that the Boks’ skipper has returned to full fitness, he has to be satisfied with being the back-up again. Despite primarily being a loose forward, Van Staden can also slot in at hooker if needed, and it looks like his versatility means he is a better option off the bench. Another player who will start on the replacements bench in this fixture is Stormers loose forward Dixon, who performed a similar role in the Boks’ three previous Tests in the Nations Championship. He has been solid whenever he has represented his country, but with Du Toit not in the squad, it was always going to be a straight shootout between him and Louw for selection as the starting blindside flanker for this game. Unfortunately for Dixon, Erasmus has opted for Louw, but he will be eager to prove a point when he eventually gets onto the field in Buenos Aires. title: Ajax v Shelbourne: Irish players and clubs have long history of lessons from Dutch masters - The Irish Times
content: When David Winner wrote Brilliant Orange: The Neurotic Genius of Dutch Football, he began with chapter five before immediately moving to chapter seven followed by chapter nine. This non-sequential numbering embodied the spirit of “Total Football”, developed by the great Ajax manager Rinus Michels, which encouraged supremely gifted players to change positions with any team-mate during a match. Its greatest practitioner was Johan Cruyff, who won consecutive European Cups with Ajax between 1971 and 1973 and whose genius enabled him to invent a new move (the Cruyff turn) named in his honour. Cruyff died in 2016 aged just 68, but a decade later, when Shelbourne visit Ajax in the Uefa Conference League on Thursday, they will still see his name everywhere. The match takes place at the 55,000-capacity Johan Cruyff Arena, where the Ajax technical director is his son Jordi, who as a player won the Premier League alongside Roy Keane and Denis Irwin with Manchester United. Irish links with Ajax have deep roots, beginning in 1910 when John Kirwan became their first professional manager. A remarkable sportsman, in 1894 aged just 17 Kirwan “won” an All-Ireland football championship with Dublin after a reply against Cork was abandoned following a brawl (the Rebels were leading by two points at the time, but refused to take part in a rescheduled third game). Kirwan then switched to soccer initially with Everton before moving to Tottenham Hotspur, who in 1901 became the only non-league side to win the FA Cup – after a replay that was actually completed. After retiring, Kirwan was lured to the Netherlands to manage Ajax. He was there for four years, guiding them to a second division title and promotion to the top flight for the first time. This elevation required Ajax to change their kit to avoid a clash with Sparta Rotterdam. Kirwan played a key role in Ajax’s adoption of their white jersey with a red vertical stripe. The Irish connection was later strengthened in 1987 when Ajax, now managed by Johan Cruyff, signed Frank Stapleton as a replacement for AC Milan-bound Marco van Basten. The honour of being signed by the greatest Dutch footballer ever, to replace the second greatest Dutch footballer ever, was somewhat undermined later when Cruyff revealed in his autobiography (inevitably called My Turn) how he had spent months attempting to sign Cyrille Regis instead. However, when Coventry City unexpectedly beat Spurs 3-2 to win the 1987 FA Cup final Regis became too expensive, so Ajax signed Stapleton instead. Cruyff explained that former Ajax team-mate Arnold Mühren had recommended Stapleton, who had played alongside him at Manchester United, and the Dubliner “didn’t cost anything, because he was still vulnerable to injury”. Stapleton only made a handful of appearances for Ajax, although his sole goal came against familiar opponents. In September 1987 Dundalk met defending champions Ajax in the first round of the European Cup Winners’ Cup. In the first leg in Amsterdam, Dundalk held out in a goalless first half with the hosts booed off and Stapleton introduced as a substitute. The change proved inspired with Ajax going on to win 4-0 with Stapleton completing the scoring. [ ‘Someone pinch me. Am I dreaming?’: When Dundalk took on Johan Cruyff’s Ajax giants ] A fortnight later a crowd of just 4,500 turned up at Oriel Park for the return leg, which Ajax won 2-0 to progress 6-0 on aggregate. The emergence of Dennis Bergkamp would see Stapleton join Derby County weeks later, but his former Ajax team-mates were not yet finished with him or Ireland. Six of that Ajax team (Frank Rijkaard, Mühren, Aron Winter, Jan Wouters, John Bosman and John van’t Schip) finished the season by winning the 1988 European Championships with the Netherlands, having previously come within minutes of a group-stage elimination before a freakish late winner by former Ajax player Wim Kieft saw them scrape a 1-0 win over a Republic of Ireland side captained by Stapleton. Off the field, Cruyff could start a row in an empty house. One journalist who complained that he could not understand a point that Cruyff was making was dismissively told: “If I wanted you to understand, I would have explained it better.” An unexpected later target for Cruyff’s ire was the FAI. In his book Cruyff revealed how in the mid-1990s he was heavily involved in the negotiations to move London club Wimbledon FC to Dublin, but “unfortunately the plan came to a standstill because the Football Association of Ireland didn’t want to co-operate”. The FAI in effect blocked the “Dublin Dons” by requiring any club based here to participate in Irish competitions. According to Cruyff, this explained why “even today Ireland has to get by without a top-level club”. Four decades later, one famous name still connects Cruyff’s outstanding Ajax team with the current one. Danny Blind scored in the 4-0 first-leg win over Dundalk and would go on to secure all three major Uefa club competitions – with Ajax winning the Cup Winners’ Cup in 1987, the Uefa Cup in 1992 and the Champions League in 1995. Last month Danny’s son Daley Blind, who has won 108 Netherlands caps, signed for Ajax for a third time. Like his father, Daley may soon find himself playing along an Irish striker as Ajax have recently been linked with a multi-million euro move for Ireland international Troy Parrott of Dutch side AZ Alkmaar and have also expressed an interest in Shamrock Rovers forward Michael Noonan, who has just turned 18. A number of players have made the reverse journey from Ajax into the League of Ireland. In 2004 midfielder Stanley Aborah began his career representing Ajax in the Champions League before finishing up in 2018 with a season at Waterford United. More recently, in 2025 Suriname international Navajo Bakboord joined Waterford, having spent more than a decade as a youth player with Ajax. The most recent League of Ireland side to visit Amsterdam were the Shamrock Rovers under-15 team, who in 2023 beat their Ajax contemporaries 2-1. Sadly one suspects that Shelbourne will discover that at senior level wiping the floor with Ajax will prove to be a much more difficult task.

title: No-Fly Lists and Federal Preemption: What Figueroa v. JetBlue Means for Airline Litigation in the Eleventh Circuit - jdsupra.com
content:
When a passenger sues an airline in state court, one of the first questions the airline’s lawyers ask is whether federal law makes the case disappear. A recent unpublished decision from a federal appeals court, reveals just how often the answer is yes — and it extends that logic to a modern feature of air travel: the airline “no-fly” list. Airlines, by their nature, operate across many jurisdictions. By the late 1970s, it was apparent that airlines could not possibly comply with often-conflicting state laws and that airline regulation needed to be centralized at the federal level. When Congress deregulated the airline industry in 1978, it wrote the following preemption clause into the Airline Deregulation Act (ADA) to prevent states from re-regulating through the back door: a state “may not enact or enforce a law …related to a price, route, or service of an air carrier.” That simple sentence has enormous reach. A claim relates to a “service” if it has a connection with, or reference to, airline services — a standard the Eleventh Circuit reads broadly. State common law counts as a “law” for these purposes, so ordinary tort and contract claims are fair game for preemption — not just formal statutes and regulations. The practical effect is that a plaintiff cannot avoid federal preemption simply by pleading a garden-variety negligence claim under state law if that claim, in substance, targets an airline’s prices, routes, or services. In Figueroa v. JetBlue Airways Corp. (11th Cir. (Fla.) July 2, 2026), Ramon Gonzalez Figueroa sued JetBlue for negligence under Florida law, alleging that JetBlue negligently placed him on its “uninvited-to-fly” list — the airline’s internal no-fly list that bars a passenger from booking future flights. The district court held that the ADA preempted the claim and dismissed it with prejudice, and he appealed the decision to the Eleventh Circuit.  A three-judge panel affirmed in a short, unsigned opinion. The court concluded that the ADA preempted Figueroa’s claim and that the district court properly dismissed his claim for good. The panel walked through the preemption clause in two steps. First, was Figueroa suing under a “law”? Yes. Florida’s common law of negligence qualifies, because state common-law rules fall comfortably within the ADA’s preemption provision. Second, was that law “related to … [the] service of an air carrier”? The Eleventh Circuit has defined an airline’s “services” to mean a bargained-for or anticipated provision of labor from the carrier to the passenger, including the transportation itself, and access to flights. When JetBlue put Figueroa on its no-fly list, it chose to deny him access to its transportation services. A claim built on that decision, the court held, plainly relates to those services and is therefore preempted by the ADA. Figueroa tried to sidestep this conclusion by analogizing to earlier Eleventh Circuit language suggesting that a claim for “wrongful removal” of a passenger from a flight might not be about a “service,” but the panel rejected that argument. His claim was not about being pulled off a plane; it was about JetBlue’s decision not to sell him tickets going forward. That decision, the court explained, speaks directly to the “economic decisions and bargained-for contractual features” of JetBlue’s business — namely, to whom the airline chooses to sell tickets. Those are exactly the kinds of market choices the ADA leaves to competition rather than state tort law. The court also affirmed the dismissal with prejudice. Figueroa argued he should be allowed to amend his complaint to add details about what happened when his flight landed, including an encounter with law enforcement. The panel determined that amendment would be futile: no additional facts would change the fundamental nature of the claim because Figueroa was placed on the list only after the flight he paid for had concluded. He was still, at bottom, complaining about JetBlue’s refusal to provide him future service — a preempted theory no matter how it was dressed up. Figueroa’s significance lies in three practical points: It confirms that “access to flights” is a preempted service. The panel treated an airline’s decision about whom it will sell tickets to as core to its “services.” That framing gives airlines a strong preemption defense whenever a plaintiff’s claim challenges a booking, boarding, or account decision — not just an in-flight event. It narrows the space left by earlier “wrongful removal” language. The Eleventh Circuit had previously suggested, in passing, that a claim for being wrongfully removed from a flight might escape preemption. Figueroa distinguishes that scenario rather than embracing it, and the court was careful to note that it was not deciding whether an actual unlawful-removal claim would survive. The takeaway for litigants: the removal exception, if it exists at all, is narrow, and it does not help a passenger challenging the denial of future service. It reinforces that recasting a claim in tort language will not defeat preemption. Figueroa pled ordinary negligence, and the court still found the claim preempted because of what it was really about. And because amendment could not cure that defect, the dismissal was with prejudice. Plaintiffs’ lawyers in the Eleventh Circuit should assume that a claim aimed at an airline’s ticketing or account decisions faces a high preemption hurdle, and that artful pleading is unlikely to clear it. For passengers, the decision is a reminder that federal law forecloses many state-court claims against airlines, even when the conduct seems like a standard tort. For airlines and their counsel, it emphasizes the legal premise that decisions about who can fly — including no-fly-list placements — fall within the ADA’s protected zone of “services.” For litigators, Figueroa signals that the Eleventh Circuit continues to read the ADA’s preemption clause expansively, leaving little room to repackage service-related disputes as ordinary negligence. Figueroa is a faithful application of binding Eleventh Circuit law and offers a clear, current window into how the court thinks about ADA preemption, which continues to shape where airline disputes can be fought and won nearly five decades after deregulation. title: Z.J.W. v. King George County School Board - ACLU of Virginia
content: We fight every day in the courts, in the legislature, and in our communities to create a Virginia for all. But we can’t do it alone. The ACLU of Virginia and Potomac Law Group filed a federal lawsuit on behalf of two students who were denied the opportunity to form a Gay Straight Alliance (GSA) at King George Middle School (KGMS) even as other noncurricular student groups were allowed to operate. Students at KGMS followed the official process to start a student club during the 2025-2026 school year, so the King George County School Board proposed new rules to make it harder to form a club as a way to block the GSA. After the ACLU of Virginia sent a letter to the school board warning that such a policy would violate federal law, the school board adopted a new policy banning all “noncurricular organizations” from forming at the middle school level – effectively barring the GSA from KGMS. Yet despite the policy’s passage, King George County Schools have continued to allow multiple noncurricular student groups to operate at the middle school level, including an outdoor club that has students making fishing lures and skinning squirrels. In fact, KGMS has attempted to define “curricular” to encompass every single club but the GSA club. The First Amendment and Equal Access Act protect all students, and the school board cannot pick and choose who the rules apply to. However, King George County Schools appears to be applying a double standard to the GSA at its middle schools. Z.J.W. v. King George School Board was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, and asks the court to issue forthcoming preliminary and permanent injunctions requiring the district to allow the GSA to form and operate on the same terms as other student organizations, as well as to prohibit the district from enforcing club policies that discriminate against student groups based on their viewpoint or retaliating against anyone who supported the GSA club. title: KRK Launches V Series Five Studio Monitors - Mixonline
content: Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now KRK's flagship V Series has been updated with new models sporting KRK Mesh wireless control and more. Nashville, TN (August 4, 2026)—KRK is launching the latest iteration of its flagship studio monitor line with the new V Series Five—three new models intended for use in recording, mixing, and immersive audio environments. Key to the new monitors is the implementation of KRK Mesh, which allows wireless control of the monitors via the KRK Control App. The compact V4 features a four-inch woofer and frequency response extending from 48 Hz to 40 kHz, with a maximum SPL of 113 dB. The V6 incorporates a 6.5-inch woofer, extends low-frequency performance to 40 Hz, and delivers up to 118 dB SPL. The largest model, the V8, has an eight-inch woofer, frequency response down to 32 Hz, and peak output of 121 dB SPL. All three models in the series feature custom-designed transducers, including woven Kevlar woofers housed in cast aluminum frames. A specially engineered one-inch silk dome tweeter provides high-frequency reproduction, and an integrated waveguide is used in an effort to provide off-axis consistency and imaging. Inside the monitors are ESS converters, Analog Devices DSP and Pascal Class D amplifier modules. Each monitor delivers 280 watts of power to the low-frequency driver and 175 watts to the high-frequency driver, providing plenty of headroom. With the onboard addition of KRK Mesh, users can wirelessly manage monitor system settings, compare EQ profiles, manage levels and optimize performance after installation without having to physically access the speaker. Whether configured as a stereo pair or as part of a larger Dolby Atmos system, the monitors can be controlled individually or grouped together. Since the monitors will be used in a variety of different applications and work environments, the speakers sport a number of room-optimization capabilities. Users can choose between 49 preset Boundary EQ combinations and seven parametric PRO EQ filters to tailor performance to the monitors’ surroundings. title: Toyota RAV4 Needs A Hail Mary To Catch Honda CR-V As America's Favorite Car - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update Toyota's Slow Start To The Year May Have Given Mazda False Hope We've included a section that focuses on Mazda's CX-5 sales in comparison to that of Toyota's RAV4. The Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V are not the largest crossover SUVs available in the US market, but they do represent the largest annual sales volume. The RAV4 has dominated sales since 2017 – representing America's best-selling vehicle without a bed – while the CR-V had the lead from 2014 to 2016. This year, there's a good chance the CR-V will reclaim the sales crown, as Toyota has dealt with tight inventories and supply-chain disruptions as the all-new sixth-generation RAV4 has rolled out, since December. The good news for Toyota fans is the RAV4 is recovering. But the bad news is it might not be enough to stave off the CR-V's challenge. It's been a slow ramp up for the RAV4, impacted this year by war with Iran choking shipments of oil and other raw materials through the Straits of Hormuz for the auto industry, stranding more than 1,000 freighters and oil tankers as of last week. ​​​​​​ Plus, Trump administration tariffs of up to 25% on vehicles imported from Canada have dinged Toyota's North American profits, as most RAV4s for the US have come from Ontario plants in Woodstock and Cambridge. As tariffs escalated, Toyota quickly scrambled to shift more RAV4 production to Georgetown, Kentucky, to protect profit margins on the automaker's best-selling vehicle. It was barely a month ago that production of the new RAV4 started in Kentucky. So now it's a race to Dec. 31 to see which SUV will be America's bestseller in 2026. Honda has a huge lead, having delivered 264,449 CR-Vs in the US through July, an increase of 8% over the same period in 2025. Meanwhile, Toyota has sold 185,240 RAV4s through July, representing a 33.7% dip from the same period in 2025. That's a gap of nearly 80,000 units to overcome in five months. Impossible? We'll see. But isolating sales just for the month of July should give Toyota and its dealers a bit of inspiration. Last month, Honda sold 38,335 CR-Vs in the US, up 18.8% from July 2025. Toyota, on the other hand, sold 31,285 RAV4s in July, down 21.3% from July 2025. For context, RAV4 sales in the US were down 48% in the first quarter to 21,693 units as the perfect storm of war with Iran and tariff pressures hindered the RAV4 launch. In that same quarter, Honda sold nearly 41,000 CR-Vs, so here's the takeaway: Toyota is closing the gap. Just as Toyota introduced a new generation of RAV4 for the 2026 model year, Mazda too launched a fresh CX-5. It's a little longer than the generation that came before it, sports an entirely new infotainment system with a slightly controversial absence of physical controls, and a sculpted new exterior design also. Sales throughout Q1 were marginally higher for the new CX-5, in comparison to 2025's figures, with 34,991 examples finding a home - 590 up on the previous year's first quarter. The tide has changed a little now though, with 12,068 sold in July 2026, compared to 15,539 in July of last year, resulting in a year-to-date figure of 74,760 - a notable 11,039 decrease in comparison to this point last year. Now that Toyota has sufficient stock of its new RAV4 model, are buyers no longer rushing to find alternative solutions at Mazda dealers, or is there another reason for CX-5 demand tailing off? Perhaps, or maybe Mazda buyers are largely holding off for the hybridized CX-5 to drop for the 2027 model year. Powertrain mix might also be a factor. At a time when volatile fuel prices are pushing shoppers into hybrids, Honda is capacity constrained for its CR-V hybrid, while every new 2026 RAV4 is a hybrid. Plug-in hybrid RAV4s are coming from Japan. But it's too early for Honda to celebrate reclaiming the sales crown with the CR-V, especially because Honda, like Toyota, also builds its midsize crossovers in Honda's Plant 2 in Alliston, Ontario, meaning those CR-Vs could be subject to tariffs as well. The upside for Honda, however, is that the automaker builds most CR-Vs for the US in East Liberty, Ohio; and Greensburg, Indiana, which nullifies tariff concerns. Even if Toyota continues a rapid production ramp-up of RAV4 in Kentucky for the next five months, the automaker will be hard-pressed to catch Honda and pass the CR-V, with its huge sales lead more than halfway through the year. After seven months, RAV4 sales are finally trending upward. But pent-demand can be a powerful thing, and there's lots of it for the all-new RAV4, as customers were told earlier in the year that it's best to place an order, rather than picking one off the lot at your neighborhood Toyota dealership. At one point this year, RAV4 inventory was "critically low," as thin as six days' supply. In metro Detroit, a quick check of local dealerships finds plentiful stocks of the new RAV4.
